lessons.title: Cleaning Masonry: Methods and Risks
lessons.body: Masonry cleaning removes dirt, soot, and biological growth from brick, stone, or concrete. But cleaning always carries risk: you can strip the protective patina, open pores, or dissolve the binder. In Africa, common soiling includes red dust from laterite, bird droppings, mould from humid coastal areas, and smoke from cooking fires. Before you start, test a small area. Use a 1:10 dilution of non-ionic detergent (like Triton X-100) in warm water. Apply with a soft natural-bristle brush, not wire. Work from bottom up to avoid streaks. Rinse with low-pressure water (under 300 psi) and a sponge. Never use high-pressure jets (over 1000 psi) on historic masonryâthey erode mortar and sandstone. For heavy soot, a poultice of kaolin clay and ammonium carbonate (1:1 by weight) can be applied 5â10 mm thick, covered with plastic, and left 24 hours. But ammonium salts can leave harmful residues; rinse thoroughly with deionised water if available. In dry regions like the Sahel, avoid wet cleaning during harmattan windsâdust will stick. In coastal areas, clean after the rainy season to remove salt. Always wear nitrile gloves, goggles, and a dust mask (N95). Work in shade; direct sun dries chemicals too fast. After cleaning, let the masonry dry 48 hours before applying any protective treatment. Remember: the goal is not to make it look new, but to remove harmful deposits while preserving historic fabric. If in doubt, leave itâdirt is often less damaging than aggressive cleaning.

lessons.title: Chemical Cleaning: Poultices and Solvents
lessons.body: Chemical cleaning uses poultices to draw out stains and solvents to dissolve coatings. A poultice is a paste that holds a cleaning agent against the surface. For masonry, mix kaolin clay or diatomaceous earth with a solvent: for oil stains, use acetone or xylene; for rust, use oxalic acid (10% solution); for biological growth, use quaternary ammonium (1:40 dilution). Apply 6â10 mm thick, cover with plastic, and leave 12â24 hours. Remove before it dries completelyâscrape into a bag and dispose as hazardous waste. For timber, use a poultice of white spirit and fuller's earth to remove wax or oil. For metal, solvents like acetone remove grease, but avoid chlorinated solvents on aluminium. In Africa, many solvents are expensive or unavailable. Local alternatives: citrus-based degreasers (d-limonene) work on light oils; vinegar (5% acetic acid) removes hard water spots on glass and glazed tile. Always test on a hidden area. Work outdoors or with cross-ventilation; solvents are flammable and toxic. Wear nitrile gloves, goggles, and a respirator with organic vapour cartridges. Do not mix chemicalsâespecially bleach and ammonia, which produce toxic gas. After poulticing, rinse with clean water and neutralise acids with baking soda solution (1 cup per litre). For stubborn soot on limestone, a poultice of ammonium carbonate and kaolin (1:3) is effective, but rinse 3â4 times. Store chemicals in original labelled containers, away from children and livestock. Dispose of residues according to local regulationsânever pour down storm drains.

lessons.title: Mechanical Cleaning: Abrasive and Laser
lessons.body: Mechanical cleaning uses physical force to remove dirt. Abrasive methods include dry grit blasting, wet grit blasting, and micro-abrasion. Grit blasting with silica sand is banned in many countries due to silicosis risk; use garnet or crushed glass instead. For historic masonry, use low pressure (2â4 bar) and a fine abrasive (0.1â0.5 mm). Keep the nozzle 300â500 mm from the surface and move continuously. Never blast mortar joints directlyâthey erode quickly. In Africa, sandblasting is common but often too aggressive. A safer alternative is the Jos/Toronto method: a fine mist of water and air at 1â2 bar with a swirl nozzle, which gently lifts dirt. For timber, use hand scrapers and bristle brushes; power sanders remove too much material. For metal, use wire brushes (brass for soft metals, steel for iron) and fine abrasive pads. Laser cleaning is emerging but expensive. A 100-watt pulsed Nd:YAG laser can remove soot from stone without touching the surface. However, lasers can cause microfractures and are not portable for large areas. In Africa, laser cleaning is rare; focus on manual and low-pressure methods. Always wear PPE: goggles, N95 mask, ear protection. Work in a contained area; use tarps to catch debris. After mechanical cleaning, vacuum with a HEPA filter to remove fine dust. Never use wire brushes on historic brickâthey scratch the fired skin. Test a small area first. If the surface becomes powdery or discoloured, stop. Mechanical cleaning is fast but irreversibleâuse it only when gentler methods fail.

lessons.title: Cleaning Timber and Metal Surfaces
lessons.body: Timber and metal need gentler cleaning than masonry. For timber, start with a soft brush and vacuum to remove loose dirt. For painted timber, use a pH-neutral detergent (1:20 dilution) and a damp clothânever soak the wood. For bare timber, remove grime with a 50:50 mix of white vinegar and water, then rinse and dry immediately. Avoid caustic soda or bleachâthey raise the grain and bleach colour. For mould on timber, use 70% isopropyl alcohol in a spray bottle; leave 10 minutes, then wipe. In humid African climates, mould returns quickly; improve ventilation and apply a borate treatment (e.g., Tim-bor) after cleaning. For metal, identify the type first. Ferrous metals (iron, steel) rust; use a wire brush or sandpaper (120â240 grit) to remove loose rust, then apply a rust converter (phosphoric acid). For non-ferrous metals (copper, brass, bronze), use a paste of lemon juice and salt, or commercial metal polish. Never use abrasive cleaners on gilded or painted metal. For aluminium, use a non-abrasive pad and mild soap. After cleaning, rinse with distilled water to avoid water spots. Dry immediately with a soft cloth. Apply a microcrystalline wax (e.g., Renaissance wax) to protect metal from tarnish; for timber, use a breathable oil like linseed or tung oil. In coastal areas, metal corrodes fastâclean and wax every 6 months. In dusty regions, cover metal with breathable fabric when not in use. Always test on a hidden area. Store brushes and cloths separately for ferrous and non-ferrous metals to avoid cross-contamination.

lessons.title: Protecting Surfaces After Cleaning
lessons.body: After cleaning, surfaces are vulnerable. Dirt and pollutants can reattach quickly, and some cleaning methods leave residues that attract new soiling. Protection starts with thorough rinsing. For masonry, rinse with deionised water if available; if not, use rain water or filtered water. Avoid tap water high in saltsâit can leave efflorescence. Let the surface dry 48â72 hours. Then apply a breathable water repellent, such as a silane/siloxane blend (e.g., 5% active ingredient). Do not use film-forming sealers (acrylic, polyurethane)âthey trap moisture and cause spalling. Apply with a low-pressure sprayer or brush, two coats, wet-on-wet. For timber, after cleaning and drying, apply a UV-resistant oil or stain. In Africa, linseed oil is cheap but can grow mould; tung oil is better. For metal, apply a microcrystalline wax or a clear lacquer (for indoor only). For all surfaces, consider a sacrificial coating: a reversible layer that can be removed later. For example, on historic stone, a lime wash (1:3 lime putty to water) can be applied and renewed every 5 years. It protects and is reversible. After protection, monitor for 6 months. Check for water beading (good) or dark patches (moisture trapped). In dusty areas, apply a anti-soiling treatment like a fluoropolymer, but these are costly. Always keep a record of products used and dates. Train local staff to reapply as needed. Remember: protection is not permanentâit is a maintenance cycle. Clean gently, protect wisely, and monitor often.

lessons.title: Case Study: Cleaning a Soot-Damaged Cathedral
lessons.body: In 2019, a 19th-century stone cathedral in Nairobi, Kenya, suffered a fire that deposited thick black soot on limestone walls and timber pews. The soot was acidic and would etch the stone if left. A team of 12 local trainees, supervised by a conservator, used a three-step process. First, dry cleaning: HEPA vacuums with soft brush attachments removed loose soot from all surfaces. Second, chemical poultice: for the limestone, they mixed kaolin clay with ammonium carbonate (1:1) and applied 8 mm thick, covered with plastic, left 18 hours. They worked in 1 mÂ² sections, from bottom up. After removal, they rinsed with deionised water three times, testing pH with litmus paper until neutral. For the timber pews, they used a poultice of fuller's earth and white spirit (1:2) to draw out embedded soot, then wiped with 70% isopropyl alcohol. Third, protection: after 72 hours drying, they applied a silane/siloxane water repellent to the stone and a tung oil finish to the timber. Challenges included limited water (they used 200 litres total, recycled for rinsing) and high humidity (they ran dehumidifiers for a week). Results: 95% of soot removed without damaging the stone's patina. Cost: about $3,500 USD for materials and 200 labour hours. Lessons: test small areas first; never use high-pressure water; control moisture; and train local people. The cathedral now has a maintenance plan: clean light soiling every 2 years, inspect for soot every 6 months. This case shows that with simple tools and careful methods, even severe soot damage can be reversed in an African context.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cleaning Buildings for Preservation â African Context

Cleaning is the highest-risk, lowest-margin phase of any preservation project. In African heritage and commercial building work â from Lamu's coral rag walls to Asmara's Modernist faÃ§ades, from Zanzibar's lime-plastered stone houses to Johannesburg's interwar masonry â the wrong cleaning method destroys the substrate, voids the client's insurance, and turns a profitable job into a liability. This reference lesson gives you the decisions, numbers, and supplier logic to quote, specify, and supervise cleaning work profitably.

1. Cleaning Masonry: Methods and Risks

Masonry in Africa rarely fails because it is dirty; it fails because cleaning removes the sacrificial layer that protected it. Coral rag on the Swahili coast, laterite in West Africa, and lime-mortared sandstone in the Sahel all share one property: they are porous and salt-active. Any method that drives water into the pore structure accelerates salt crystallisation and, in coastal zones, chloride-driven corrosion of embedded iron.

Before quoting, classify the soiling:

  • Atmospheric soiling â carbonaceous crust, common on urban faÃ§ades in Cairo, Nairobi, and Johannesburg.
  • Biological â algae, lichen, mould; heavy in humid zones (Mombasa, Douala, Lagos).
  • Salt efflorescence â white bloom, cyclical, needs poultice not washing.
  • Paint and graffiti â often the client's real complaint.
  • Soot and fire damage â see the cathedral case study below.

Commercial risk is asymmetric. A trial panel costs you a day; a failed faÃ§ade costs you the contract, the retention, and your reputation with the heritage authority. Always price trial panels as a separate line item â clients accept this when you explain it protects their asset value.

Table 1. Masonry cleaning methods â suitability and risk by substrate
Method Suitable substrate Primary risk Indicative cost (USD/mÂ², 2024)
Low-pressure water (<50 bar) Dense stone, brick, concrete Salt mobilisation, efflorescence 3â8
Steam (controlled) Lime plaster, painted surfaces Binder loss if overheated 6â14
Poultice (clay/paper pulp) Salt-loaded masonry, stone Incomplete extraction, re-deposit 10â25
Solvent gel Graffiti, paint on stone Solvent ingress, VOC exposure 12â30
Abrasive (fine grit) Dense, non-carved stone Surface loss, loss of tool marks 8â20
Laser (Nd:YAG, Q-switched) Delicate carved stone, metal Over-cleaning, colour change 40â120

Costs are indicative contractor rates for sub-Saharan Africa; source: author's compilation from regional tenders and Historic England guidance on cleaning.

2. Chemical Cleaning: Poultices and Solvents

Poultices work by capillary action: a moist paste draws soluble salts and soiling out of the pore structure as it dries. The technique is old, cheap, and unforgiving. The two failure modes are too wet (drives salts deeper) and too dry (nothing moves). For salt-loaded coral or lime, use a clay-kaolin or paper-pulp poultice with deionised water, applied 10â20 mm thick, covered to slow drying, and removed at the leather-hard stage.

Solvents are for organic soiling â paints, oils, graffiti. In Africa, solvent supply chains are the constraint: import lead times and customs clearance can add 3â6 weeks. Specify products available locally where possible, or price the lead time into your programme. Always check the safety data sheet (SDS) and confirm VOC limits against the client's site rules and local environmental regulations.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICAL CLEANING

Solvents, biocides, and alkaline cleaners are hazardous. In hot African climates, evaporation concentrates vapours and increases inhalation risk. Mandatory controls:

  • Never mix bleach and acid â releases chlorine gas. Fatal in enclosed courtyards.
  • Use full-face respirators with correct cartridges (organic vapour or acid gas), not dust masks.
  • Provide forced ventilation in courtyards, atria, and basements; monitor with a gas detector.
  • Eye wash and running water within 10 seconds of the work face.
  • Store solvents away from direct sun; temperatures above 35 Â°C raise vapour pressure dangerously.
  • Dispose of poultice and rinse water as hazardous waste â never into storm drains.

3. Mechanical Cleaning: Abrasive and Laser

Abrasive cleaning is fast and cheap, which is exactly why it is over-used. On carved stone, abrasive blasting erases tool marks â the very evidence that gives a building its heritage value and, in commercial terms, its listing status and grant eligibility. The rule: if the surface has any carving, moulding, or historic finish, abrasive is off the table unless a trial panel proves otherwise.

Laser cleaning (Nd:YAG, Q-switched) is the premium option. It is dry, precise, and ideal for soot, metal, and delicate stone. In Africa, the constraint is equipment access: machines are typically hired from South Africa or Europe, with mobilisation costs of USD 3,000â8,000. For a cathedral or museum contract, this is justifiable; for a single faÃ§ade, it rarely is. Price laser as a specialist sub-contract, not as an in-house service.

Table 2. Mechanical cleaning â selection matrix
Technique Best for Do not use on Productivity (mÂ²/day)
Dry grit blasting Heavy carbon crust, dense concrete Carved stone, lime, timber 80â150
Wet grit / slurry Dense masonry, dust control Salt-active substrates 60â100
Micro-abrasion (fine nozzle) Detail work, small areas Soft stone, painted surfaces 10â25
Rotary brush / bristle Loose soiling, biological Friable or flaking surfaces 40â80
Laser (Nd:YAG) Soot, metal, delicate carving Some pigments, certain metals 2â8

Productivity figures are field estimates for a two-person crew; source: author's compilation from contractor data and Historic England technical guidance.

4. Cleaning Timber and Metal Surfaces

Timber. Never wet-clean historic timber. Moisture raises the risk of fungal decay and dimensional movement, and in tropical Africa, termites follow damp wood. Dry-brush with soft bristles, vacuum with HEPA filtration, and use a conservation-grade poultice only for localised stains. If the timber is painted, test for lead before any abrasion â pre-1970s paint in many African cities contains lead.

Metal. Ferrous metal: remove corrosion products by hand, apply a rust converter only where specified, and protect immediately. Non-ferrous (copper, brass, bronze): do not polish to a bright finish unless the client's brief and the heritage authority explicitly require it â patina is part of the significance. In coastal Africa, salt-laden air means any bare metal will re-corrode within weeks; protection must be applied the same day as cleaning.

5. Protecting Surfaces After Cleaning

Cleaning without protection is a maintenance liability you have just handed to the client. Match the protection to the substrate:

  • Masonry: breathable water repellent (silane/siloxane), never a film-forming acrylic. Test for colour change.
  • Timber: breathable oil or microporous stain; avoid polyurethane on historic joinery.
  • Metal: wax or lacquer for non-ferrous; primer plus topcoat for ferrous.
  • All: document the protection product, batch, and application date in the O&M manual â this is a billable deliverable and protects you from future blame.

6. Case Study: Cleaning a Soot-Damaged Cathedral

A 19th-century stone cathedral in an African capital suffered a major fire. Soot and pyrolytic carbon bonded to limestone, lime plaster, and stained glass. The client's insurer required documented method statements and a conservation-accredited supervisor.

Approach: (1) Dry HEPA vacuuming to remove loose soot; (2) poultice cleaning on salt-loaded limestone; (3) laser cleaning on carved capitals and stained-glass surrounds; (4) micro-abrasion only on flat, unadorned plinth stone; (5) breathable water repellent after 14 days of drying.

Commercial outcome: the laser sub-contract was 22% of the cleaning budget but unlocked the heritage grant, which covered 40% of the total project. The lesson for African contractors: the premium method is often the one that makes the project fundable. Price the method against the funding, not just the labour.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Substrate and soiling identified in writing before any method is specified.
  2. Trial panel completed (minimum 1 mÂ²), photographed, and signed off by client and heritage authority.
  3. Method statement and risk assessment approved, including lead and asbestos screening.
  4. PPE, ventilation, and eye-wash station in place; SDS available on site.
  5. Water pressure, grit grade, or laser fluence recorded and locked to the approved trial.
  6. Stop conditions agreed in writing â substrate loss, colour shift, salt return.
  7. Protection applied same day (metal) or after specified drying (masonry, timber).
  8. Cleaning and protection documented in the O&M manual with product and batch data.

Further Reading

  • Historic England â Practical Building Conservation series (free guidance)
  • ICOMOS â International Charters and Technical Guidance (free)
  • Getty Conservation Institute â free publications on cleaning and conservation
  • ICCROM â free resources on heritage conservation practice
  • UNESCO World Heritage Centre â Operational Guidelines (free)

Rise AFRICA Skills note: Cleaning is a service business. Sell the trial panel, the documentation, and the protection as separate value lines â they are what separate a contractor who gets repeat heritage work from one who gets one job and a complaint.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum water pressure for cleaning historic masonry?
quiz.explanation: High pressure above 300 psi can erode mortar and damage historic masonry.

quiz.q: Which tool should never be used on historic brick?
quiz.explanation: Wire brushes scratch the fired skin of historic brick, causing irreversible damage.

quiz.q: What is a poultice?
options: B) A paste that holds a cleaning agent against a surface
C) A type of abrasive blasting
quiz.explanation: A poultice is a paste applied to draw out stains and hold chemicals in place.

quiz.q: Which chemical is commonly used in a poultice for rust stains?
quiz.explanation: Oxalic acid (10% solution) is effective for removing rust stains from masonry.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing bleach and ammonia?
options: A) It creates a bad smell
quiz.explanation: Mixing bleach and ammonia releases chloramine gas, which is highly toxic.

quiz.q: What is a safer alternative to silica sand for abrasive blasting?
quiz.explanation: Crushed glass or garnet avoids the silicosis risk associated with silica sand.

quiz.q: What is the recommended nozzle distance for grit blasting historic masonry?
quiz.explanation: Keeping the nozzle 300â500 mm away reduces damage to the surface.

quiz.q: Which method is described as gentle and uses a fine mist of water and air?
quiz.explanation: The Jos/Toronto method uses low-pressure water and air to gently lift dirt.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean mould from timber?
quiz.explanation: Isopropyl alcohol kills mould without bleaching or raising the grain of the wood.

quiz.q: What is a suitable protective coating for metal after cleaning?
quiz.explanation: Microcrystalline wax protects metal from tarnish without forming a permanent film.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid film-forming sealers on historic masonry?
options: B) They trap moisture and cause spalling
C) They are not available in Africa
quiz.explanation: Film-forming sealers trap moisture, which can lead to spalling and deterioration.

quiz.q: What is a sacrificial coating?
options: B) A reversible layer that can be removed later
quiz.explanation: A sacrificial coating is designed to be renewed and removed without damaging the original surface.

quiz.q: In the Nairobi cathedral case study, what was used to neutralise the stone after poulticing?
quiz.explanation: They rinsed with deionised water until the pH was neutral.

quiz.q: How long did the team leave the poultice on the limestone in the case study?
quiz.explanation: They left the poultice for 18 hours to draw out the soot.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cleaning soot-damaged surfaces?
options: B) Dry cleaning with HEPA vacuum
quiz.explanation: Dry cleaning removes loose soot before any wet methods are used.

quiz.q: Which of these is a local alternative for degreasing?
quiz.explanation: Citrus-based degreasers (d-limonene) are effective and less toxic.

quiz.q: What PPE is essential when using solvents?
quiz.explanation: Nitrile gloves and a respirator with organic vapour cartridges protect against solvent exposure.

quiz.q: How often should metal be cleaned and waxed in coastal areas?
quiz.explanation: Coastal salt accelerates corrosion, so cleaning and waxing every 6 months is recommended.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dilution for a non-ionic detergent for masonry cleaning?
quiz.explanation: A 1:10 dilution of non-ionic detergent in warm water is effective and gentle.

quiz.q: Why should you work from bottom up when cleaning masonry?
quiz.explanation: Working bottom up prevents dirty water from streaking already cleaned areas.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of using ammonium carbonate poultices?
quiz.explanation: Ammonium salts can leave residues that may damage the masonry if not thoroughly rinsed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mechanical cleaning method?
quiz.explanation: Grit blasting is an abrasive mechanical method that uses physical force.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of laser cleaning?
options: B) It removes soot without touching the surface
C) It works on all materials
quiz.explanation: Laser cleaning is non-contact and can remove soot without abrasion.

quiz.q: What should you do after mechanical cleaning?
quiz.explanation: HEPA vacuuming removes fine dust that could be harmful or cause re-soiling.

quiz.q: For cleaning bare timber, what is a safe mixture?
quiz.explanation: A 50:50 mix of white vinegar and water removes grime without damaging the wood.

quiz.q: What is a suitable protective treatment for timber after cleaning?
quiz.explanation: Tung oil is a breathable, UV-resistant finish suitable for timber.

quiz.q: How long should you let masonry dry after cleaning before applying a protective treatment?
quiz.explanation: Masonry should dry for 48â72 hours to allow moisture to escape before sealing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a silane/siloxane water repellent?
options: A) To seal the surface completely
B) To allow breathability while repelling water
quiz.explanation: Silane/siloxane penetrates and repels water while still allowing vapour to escape.

quiz.q: In the case study, what was the total cost of the cleaning project?
quiz.explanation: The case study states the cost was about $3,500 USD for materials and labour.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson from the cathedral case study?
options: B) Test small areas and train local people
quiz.explanation: The case study emphasizes testing, gentle methods, and local training.
